note: First-party curated BPMN 2.0 knowledge base for generating grounded C1 (Q&A/tutor) training data. Facts authored from BPMN 2.0 knowledge; treat as needs-human-review. Each entry may provide: definition, notation, when_to_use, contrast {term, how}.

concepts.definition: A start event indicates where a process begins; it is a source of a token and has no incoming sequence flow.
concepts.notation: a thin single-line circle, empty for a 'none' start or with an internal marker for a typed trigger (message, timer, signal, etc.).
concepts.when_to_use: to mark the trigger that instantiates a process or sub-process.

concepts.definition: An end event indicates where a path of a process ends; it consumes a token and has no outgoing sequence flow.
concepts.notation: a thick single-line circle, empty for a 'none' end or with a marker for a result (message, error, terminate, etc.).

concepts.definition: An intermediate event occurs between the start and end of a process, either catching a trigger or throwing a result as the flow passes through it.
concepts.notation: a double-line (two thin concentric) circle with an optional trigger marker.

concepts.definition: A message event represents the sending or receiving of a message between participants.
concepts.notation: an envelope marker inside the event circle (unfilled when catching, filled when throwing).

contrast.how: a message is directed to one specific receiver (1-to-1), whereas a signal is broadcast to any listener (1-to-many).

concepts.definition: A timer event fires based on a temporal condition such as a specific date, an elapsed duration, or a recurring cycle; it is always catching.
concepts.notation: a clock symbol inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: An error event represents a named error being thrown (at the end of a sub-process) or caught (on a boundary or in an event sub-process); catching an error is always interrupting.
concepts.notation: a lightning-bolt / jagged-arrow marker inside the event circle.

contrast.how: an error is a critical, always-interrupting failure, whereas an escalation signals a situation needing attention and can be interrupting or non-interrupting.

concepts.definition: A terminate end event immediately ends all activity in the process instance (or the current sub-process level), discarding any remaining tokens.
concepts.notation: a solid filled circle inside the end event.

contrast.how: a none end event only consumes the arriving token and lets other parallel tokens continue, while a terminate end event stops the whole process level at once.

concepts.definition: An exclusive (XOR) gateway routes a token to exactly one of its outgoing paths based on data conditions; on converging it passes each incoming token through without synchronisation.
concepts.notation: a diamond, optionally with an 'X' marker.
concepts.when_to_use: to model a decision where exactly one alternative path is taken.

concepts.definition: A parallel (AND) gateway creates concurrent paths on diverging (all outgoing flows activate) and synchronises them on converging (waits for a token on every incoming flow); it never evaluates conditions.
concepts.notation: a diamond with a '+' marker.
concepts.when_to_use: to run activities concurrently and then wait for all of them to finish.

concepts.definition: An inclusive (OR) gateway activates every outgoing path whose condition is true (one or more), and on converging waits for all activated incoming paths.
concepts.notation: a diamond with a circle 'O' marker.

contrast.how: an exclusive gateway takes exactly one path, while an inclusive gateway may take several paths at once.

concepts.definition: An event-based gateway routes based on which of several following catching events occurs first, rather than on data conditions.
concepts.notation: a diamond containing a pentagon inside a double circle.
concepts.when_to_use: to model a race between events, e.g. wait for a reply message or a timeout, whichever happens first.

concepts.definition: A complex gateway models routing behaviour too intricate for the other gateways, using an activation/completion condition (e.g. proceed once 3 of 5 branches complete).
concepts.notation: a diamond with an asterisk '*' marker.

concepts.definition: A user task is work performed by a human with the support of a software application, managed by the process engine and typically appearing on a task list.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a small person icon.

contrast.how: a user task is engine-managed software-assisted work, while a manual task is done with no engine or application involvement.

concepts.definition: A service task is work performed automatically by a system or service, such as calling an API or running business logic, with no human involvement.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a gears/cog icon.
concepts.when_to_use: for fully automated steps executed by software.

concepts.definition: A script task is executed by the process engine running a script written in a language the engine can interpret.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a script (scroll) icon.

concepts.definition: A business rule task sends inputs to a business-rules or decision engine (often DMN) and receives a decision, keeping decision logic separate from the flow.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a table/grid icon.

concepts.definition: A send task is an activity whose completion is the sending of a message to another participant.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a filled envelope icon.

contrast.how: a send task dispatches a message, whereas a receive task waits for and consumes an incoming message.

concepts.definition: A receive task waits for a message from another participant and completes when it arrives; with instantiate set true it can start a process.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with an unfilled envelope icon.

concepts.definition: A sub-process is a compound activity that contains its own flow of elements, used to group and encapsulate part of a process; it can be collapsed or expanded.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle; when collapsed it shows a '+' marker at the bottom-centre.

contrast.how: a sub-process is defined inline within its parent, while a call activity invokes a separate, reusable global process or task.

concepts.definition: A call activity is a wrapper that invokes a reusable, globally-defined process or global task from within the current process.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a thick (bold) border.

concepts.definition: A transaction is a specialised sub-process whose contained work either completes successfully as a unit or is compensated/cancelled together.
concepts.notation: a sub-process drawn with a double-lined border; a cancel event may be attached to its boundary.

concepts.definition: An ad-hoc sub-process contains activities that may be executed in any order, repeated, or skipped until a completion condition is met, with no mandatory sequence flow between them.
concepts.notation: a sub-process with a tilde '~' marker at the bottom-centre.

concepts.definition: A boundary event is attached to the edge of an activity and reacts to a trigger (error, timer, message, signal, escalation, etc.) while that activity is running.
concepts.notation: a circle on the activity's border; a solid border is interrupting, a dashed border is non-interrupting.

concepts.definition: An event sub-process is placed inside a process or sub-process and is triggered by a start event rather than by incoming sequence flow, used for in-scope event and exception handling.
concepts.notation: a sub-process drawn with a dotted border, begun by an interrupting (solid) or non-interrupting (dashed) start event.

concepts.definition: A pool represents a participant in a collaboration — an organisation, system, or role — and contains at most one process.
concepts.notation: a large rectangle, usually labelled on a shaded side band.

contrast.how: a pool is a participant boundary that message flows cross, while a lane is a sub-partition within one pool that sequence flow may cross freely.

concepts.definition: A lane is a sub-partition within a pool used to organise and categorise activities, typically by role, department, or system; it has no execution semantics.
concepts.notation: a horizontal or vertical band subdividing a pool.

concepts.definition: A sequence flow defines the order in which activities are performed within a single process (within one pool).
concepts.notation: a solid line with a solid arrowhead.

contrast.how: a sequence flow orders activities inside one participant, while a message flow shows communication between two different participants and cannot connect elements in the same pool.

concepts.definition: A message flow shows the exchange of a message between two separate participants (pools).
concepts.notation: a dashed line with an open circle at the source and an open arrowhead at the target.

concepts.definition: A data object represents information required or produced by activities; it exists only for the duration of the process instance.
concepts.notation: a page/rectangle with a folded top-right corner.

contrast.how: a data object lives only for the process instance, while a data store persists information beyond the instance.

concepts.definition: A data store is a place where the process can read or write persistent information that outlives any single process instance.
concepts.notation: a cylinder (database) symbol.

concepts.definition: A text annotation is an artifact that adds explanatory notes to a diagram; it does not affect the flow.
concepts.notation: an open bracket shape connected to an element by a dotted association.

concepts.definition: A group is an artifact that visually clusters related elements for documentation or analysis; it has no effect on the sequence flow and may cross pools and lanes.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle with a dashed dot-dash border.

concepts.definition: Compensation undoes the effect of an already-completed activity, for example reversing a payment that was charged; it is triggered after the activity has finished successfully.
concepts.notation: a 'rewind' marker of two left-pointing triangles, used on an activity or inside an event.

concepts.definition: A conditional flow is a sequence flow carrying a condition expression that must evaluate to true for the flow to be taken.
concepts.notation: when leaving an activity directly it is drawn with a small diamond marker at its source.

concepts.definition: A default flow is the outgoing path taken from an exclusive or inclusive gateway (or an activity) only when no other outgoing condition evaluates to true.
concepts.notation: a sequence flow marked with a small back-slash tick near its source.

concepts.definition: A signal event throws or catches a signal that is broadcast to any interested listener, not directed to a single receiver.
concepts.notation: a triangle marker inside the event circle (filled when throwing, unfilled when catching).
concepts.when_to_use: to coordinate across multiple processes or paths that should all react to the same occurrence.

concepts.definition: An escalation event signals that a situation needs a higher level of attention or intervention; unlike an error it can be interrupting or non-interrupting and need not abort the activity.
concepts.notation: an upward-pointing open arrowhead marker inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: A cancel event is used only with a transaction sub-process: it is thrown to abort the transaction and caught on the transaction's boundary to trigger compensation and cleanup.
concepts.notation: an 'X' marker inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: A conditional event fires when a defined business condition (a boolean expression over data) becomes true; it is catch-only.
concepts.notation: a lined-list (mini form) marker inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: A link event connects two sections of a process within the same level as a paired throw/catch, acting as an off-page connector to avoid long crossing sequence flows.
concepts.notation: an arrow marker inside the event circle (filled for the throwing source, unfilled for the catching target).

concepts.definition: A multiple event has more than one assigned trigger; when catching, any one of the triggers fires it, and when throwing, all of its triggers are produced.
concepts.notation: a pentagon marker inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: A parallel multiple catching event fires only when ALL of its assigned triggers have occurred, unlike a multiple event which fires on any one.
concepts.notation: a plus-sign (cross) marker inside the event circle.

concepts.definition: A message start event instantiates a process when a specific message is received.
concepts.notation: a thin-line start circle containing an unfilled envelope.

concepts.definition: A timer start event instantiates a process at a specified time or on a recurring schedule.
concepts.notation: a thin-line start circle containing a clock symbol.

concepts.definition: An error end event ends its path by throwing a named error, which is expected to be caught by an error boundary event or error event sub-process on an enclosing scope.
concepts.notation: a thick-line end circle containing a filled lightning-bolt marker.

concepts.definition: An activity is a unit of work performed in a process; it can be atomic (a task) or compound (a sub-process), and is the general term for the 'work' shapes.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle.

concepts.definition: A loop activity (standard loop) repeats while (or until) a boolean loop condition holds, evaluating the condition before or after each iteration.
concepts.notation: a circular-arrow marker at the bottom-centre of the activity.

contrast.how: a standard loop repeats sequentially based on a condition, while a multi-instance activity runs a known number of instances (often over a collection), sequentially or in parallel.

concepts.definition: A multi-instance activity executes multiple instances of the same activity, typically once per item in a collection, either in parallel or in sequence.
concepts.notation: three vertical bars (parallel) or three horizontal bars (sequential) at the bottom-centre.

concepts.definition: A global task is a reusable, standalone task definition declared at the model level that can be invoked from multiple processes via a call activity.
concepts.when_to_use: to define a common task once and reuse it across several processes.

concepts.definition: The isForCompensation attribute on an activity marks it as a compensation handler that runs only when compensation is triggered, not as part of the normal flow.
A gateway controls how sequence flow diverges (splits) or converges (merges) in a process; the internal marker and type determine the routing behaviour.
concepts.notation: a diamond shape.

concepts.definition: A diverging (split) gateway has one incoming and multiple outgoing sequence flows, distributing the flow according to its type.

contrast.how: a diverging gateway splits one path into several, while a converging gateway merges several paths into one.

concepts.definition: A converging (merge/join) gateway has multiple incoming and one outgoing sequence flow, combining paths according to its type (e.g. a parallel gateway synchronises, an exclusive gateway passes each token through).
The gatewayDirection attribute declares a gateway's intended use — Unspecified, Converging, Diverging, or Mixed — to document and constrain how many incoming/outgoing flows it has.
A token is a theoretical object that traverses the sequence flows and passes through elements to describe how a process executes; start events create tokens and end events consume them.
concepts.when_to_use: to reason about concurrency and completion — e.g. a parallel gateway split creates one token per outgoing branch.

concepts.definition: Normal flow is the sequence-flow path from a start event through activities to an end event, not including exception or compensation handling.
Exception flow is the path taken out of an activity when an (interrupting) boundary event fires, diverting the token away from the normal flow to handle the error or condition.
A collaboration shows two or more participants (pools) and the message flows exchanged between them.
concepts.notation: multiple pools connected by dashed message flows.

contrast.how: an orchestration (private process) models the internal flow of a single participant, while a collaboration models the interaction between participants.

concepts.definition: A choreography defines the expected sequence of message exchanges between participants, focusing on the interactions themselves rather than any participant's internal work.
concepts.notation: a sequence of choreography tasks, each a rounded rectangle banded with participant names.

concepts.definition: A choreography task represents one interaction — a message exchange between two participants — within a choreography.
concepts.notation: a rounded rectangle split into bands naming the initiating and receiving participants.

concepts.definition: A conversation diagram is a simplified view of a collaboration that groups related message exchanges between participants into named conversations.
concepts.notation: a hexagon linking participant pools.

concepts.definition: A participant is a business entity (organisation, role, or system) that takes part in a collaboration and is represented by a pool.

contrast.how: a participant is the modelled entity; a pool is the graphical container that represents that participant in the diagram.

concepts.definition: A black-box pool is a participant pool shown without any internal process detail, used when only its message interactions matter.
concepts.when_to_use: to represent an external party (e.g. a customer or third-party system) whose internals are unknown or irrelevant.

concepts.definition: A message represents the content of a communication between two participants and is associated with a message flow.
concepts.notation: a small envelope shape, optionally shown on a message flow.

concepts.definition: Correlation is the mechanism that routes an incoming message to the specific running process instance it belongs to, typically by matching a key in the message payload.
A data input declares data that an activity or process requires before it can execute, as part of its InputOutputSpecification.

contrast.how: a data input is data consumed before execution, while a data output is data produced when the activity completes.

concepts.definition: A data output declares data that an activity or process produces on completion, as part of its InputOutputSpecification.
A data association moves data between data objects/stores/inputs/outputs and the activities that use them, optionally applying a transformation.
concepts.notation: a dotted line with an open arrowhead (a directed association).

concepts.definition: An ItemDefinition defines the structure (type) of the data items carried by data objects, messages, and properties — for example referencing an XSD type.
concepts.when_to_use: to give data objects and messages a concrete data type for execution.

concepts.definition: A property holds data local to a process or activity that is not visualised as a data object, often used to carry values during execution.
An association links artifacts (such as text annotations or data) to flow elements without affecting the execution flow.
concepts.notation: a dotted line, with an arrowhead only when direction is meaningful.

contrast.how: an association is a non-executing link to artifacts/data, while a sequence flow defines the order of execution between flow nodes.

concepts.definition: An artifact provides additional information on a diagram without affecting the flow; the standard artifacts are text annotations and groups (associations connect them).
The documentation element is a model attribute attachable to almost any BPMN element to hold descriptive text; it is stored in the XML and not rendered on the diagram.

contrast.how: documentation is invisible model metadata, while a text annotation is a visible note drawn on the diagram.

concepts.definition: Extension elements allow vendor- or organisation-specific data to be attached to BPMN elements without breaking standard compliance, using a namespaced extension.
concepts.when_to_use: to store engine-specific configuration (e.g. Camunda properties) alongside standard BPMN.

concepts.definition: A process is a sequence of activities, events, and gateways performed within a single participant to achieve a business outcome.
concepts.notation: the flow content inside a single pool (or a pool-less diagram).

concepts.definition: A private (internal) process is the internal workflow of a single organisation, showing its own activities and control flow.

contrast.how: a private process shows all internal activities, while a public process shows only the activities that interact with other participants, hiding internal detail.

concepts.definition: A public process shows only the flow elements of a participant that communicate with other participants, hiding purely internal steps.
A flow element is any element that appears in the flow of a process — events, activities, gateways, sequence flows, and data elements are all flow elements.
A flow node is a flow element that can be connected by sequence flow — namely an event, activity, or gateway (sequence flows and data are not flow nodes).
A lane set is the collection of lanes that partition a process or a lane; a process can contain a lane set to organise its flow nodes into lanes.
A resource is a reusable definition of who or what can perform work (e.g. a role or group), which activities reference to assign performers.

contrast.how: a resource is the reusable definition, while a performer is the assignment of that resource (in a role such as potential owner) to a specific activity.

concepts.definition: A performer specifies the resource responsible for an activity; for human tasks, specialised performers such as the potential owner determine who may claim the work.
A compensation handler is an activity (marked isForCompensation) associated with a compensation boundary event that runs to undo the effects of the activity it compensates.
concepts.notation: linked to a compensation boundary event by an association (not a sequence flow).

concepts.definition: A throwing event produces (emits) a trigger such as a message, signal, or escalation as the token passes through it.
concepts.notation: a filled (dark) trigger marker inside the event.

contrast.how: a throwing event actively emits a trigger, while a catching event waits for and reacts to a trigger.

concepts.definition: A catching event waits for a trigger (such as a message arriving or a timer elapsing) before the flow continues past it.
concepts.notation: an unfilled (open) trigger marker inside the event.

concepts.definition: A none event carries no trigger type; a none start event begins a process on demand and a none end event simply marks the end of a path.
concepts.notation: an event circle with no internal marker.

concepts.definition: standardLoopCharacteristics is the child element that turns an activity into a standard loop, holding the loop condition and whether it is tested before or after each iteration.

contrast.how: standardLoopCharacteristics repeats while a condition holds, whereas multiInstanceLoopCharacteristics runs a fixed set of instances (often over a collection).

concepts.definition: multiInstanceLoopCharacteristics is the child element that makes an activity multi-instance, specifying the number of instances (or a collection), sequential vs parallel execution, and an optional completion condition.
concepts.when_to_use: when the same activity must run once per item in a collection.

concepts.definition: isSequential is a boolean on multi-instance characteristics: true runs the instances one after another, false runs them in parallel.

contrast.how: isSequential controls ordering of instances, while loopCardinality sets how many instances there are.

concepts.definition: loopCardinality is an expression giving the number of instances a multi-instance activity should create.
concepts.when_to_use: when the instance count is known numerically rather than derived from a data collection.

concepts.definition: completionCondition is an expression on a multi-instance or ad-hoc activity that, when true, stops creating/continuing instances even if others remain.
concepts.when_to_use: to short-circuit a multi-instance activity once enough instances have finished (e.g. 3 of 5 approvals).

concepts.definition: loopCondition is the boolean expression evaluated by a standard loop to decide whether to run another iteration.
concepts.when_to_use: to repeat an activity until a business condition is satisfied.

concepts.definition: testBefore is a boolean on standardLoopCharacteristics: true evaluates the loop condition before the first iteration (while-loop), false evaluates after (do-while), guaranteeing at least one run.
concepts.when_to_use: set false when the activity must always execute at least once.

concepts.definition: cancelActivity is a boolean on a boundary event: true makes it interrupting (the attached activity is cancelled when it fires), false makes it non-interrupting (the activity keeps running).

contrast.how: cancelActivity controls interrupting behaviour for boundary events, while isInterrupting controls it for event sub-process start events.

concepts.definition: isInterrupting is a boolean on an event sub-process's start event: true cancels the enclosing process when triggered, false lets it continue in parallel.
concepts.when_to_use: set false for event handlers that should run alongside the main flow.

concepts.definition: triggeredByEvent is a boolean on a sub-process: when true it marks the sub-process as an event sub-process, started by an event rather than incoming sequence flow.
concepts.when_to_use: to declare in-scope event/exception handling inside a process.

concepts.definition: An eventDefinition child element gives an event its trigger type — for example messageEventDefinition, timerEventDefinition, errorEventDefinition, or signalEventDefinition.
concepts.when_to_use: an event with no eventDefinition is a 'none' event; add one to type the trigger.

concepts.definition: messageRef references the specific message that a message event or message flow carries.

contrast.how: messageRef points to a directed message (1-to-1), while signalRef points to a broadcast signal (1-to-many).

concepts.definition: errorRef references the specific named Error that an error event throws or catches, enabling matching between a thrown error and its handler.
concepts.when_to_use: to catch a particular error rather than any error.

concepts.definition: signalRef references the specific Signal that a signal event throws or catches; all catchers listening for that signal react when it is broadcast.
concepts.when_to_use: to coordinate multiple listeners on a named signal.

concepts.definition: completionQuantity is the number of tokens that must be produced for an activity to be considered complete (default 1).

contrast.how: startQuantity is how many tokens must arrive to begin the activity, while completionQuantity is how many must be produced to finish it.

concepts.definition: startQuantity is the number of tokens that must arrive on incoming sequence flow before an activity begins (default 1).
calledElement on a call activity references the reusable global process or global task that the call activity invokes.
concepts.when_to_use: to point a call activity at the reusable definition it should execute.

concepts.definition: isCollection is a boolean on a data object (or item) indicating it represents a collection of items rather than a single item.
concepts.notation: a small parallel-bars (collection) marker on the data object.

concepts.definition: A dataState on a data object captures the lifecycle state of the data (e.g. 'received', 'approved'), often shown in square brackets after the name.
concepts.notation: the state shown in [brackets] beneath or after the data object label.

concepts.definition: An inputSet defines a valid combination of data inputs required together for an activity to start, within its InputOutputSpecification.

contrast.how: an inputSet describes valid input combinations before execution, an outputSet describes valid output combinations after.

concepts.definition: An outputSet defines a valid combination of data outputs an activity produces on completion, within its InputOutputSpecification.
sourceRef on a sequence flow (or message flow) identifies the element the connection starts from.

contrast.how: sourceRef is the origin element of a flow, targetRef is the destination element.

concepts.definition: targetRef on a sequence flow (or message flow) identifies the element the connection points to.
The default attribute on an exclusive/inclusive gateway (or activity) names which outgoing sequence flow is the default path, taken when no condition is true.
concepts.when_to_use: to guarantee a fall-through path and avoid a stuck token when no condition matches.

concepts.definition: instantiate is a boolean marking a receive task or event-based gateway as able to start a new process instance on the first message/event.
concepts.when_to_use: to begin a process on message receipt without a separate message start event.

concepts.definition: A conditionExpression on a sequence flow is the boolean expression evaluated to decide whether that flow is taken out of a gateway or activity.
concepts.when_to_use: on the outgoing flows of exclusive/inclusive gateways to encode the routing logic.

concepts.definition: A formalExpression is an expression written in a formal language (identified by a language URI, e.g. an expression language) that an engine can evaluate, used for conditions, loop cardinalities, and the like.

contrast.how: a formalExpression is machine-evaluable, while an informal (plain Expression) is human-readable text not meant for automatic evaluation.

concepts.definition: targetNamespace on the definitions root scopes all elements defined in the file to a namespace URI, keeping ids unique across imported models.
concepts.when_to_use: to uniquely qualify a model so its elements can be referenced from other files.

concepts.definition: The id attribute is the unique identifier of a BPMN element within its document; sequence flows and diagram elements reference elements by id.
concepts.when_to_use: must be unique — duplicate ids make references ambiguous and the file invalid.

concepts.definition: The definitions element is the root of a BPMN 2.0 XML file, containing processes, collaborations, messages, and the diagram interchange, and declaring the namespaces used.
concepts.notation: not drawn; it is the top-level XML container.

concepts.definition: A rootElement is a top-level element directly under definitions — for example a process, collaboration, message, error, or signal — that can be referenced across the model.
BPMNDiagram is the DI element that holds the visual representation of a model, containing a BPMNPlane with the shapes and edges.
concepts.when_to_use: present in the XML so tools can render the model consistently.

concepts.definition: BPMNPlane is the DI container inside a BPMNDiagram that holds all the BPMNShape and BPMNEdge elements for a given process or collaboration.

contrast.how: a BPMNDiagram is the whole picture, while a BPMNPlane is the drawing surface within it that holds the shapes.

concepts.definition: A BPMNShape is the DI element giving the position and size (via a Bounds) of a single flow node such as an event, activity, or gateway.
concepts.notation: references its model element through the bpmnElement attribute.

concepts.definition: A BPMNEdge is the DI element describing the route of a connection (sequence flow, message flow, or association) as a list of waypoints.

contrast.how: a BPMNShape lays out a node's box, while a BPMNEdge lays out a connection's line.

concepts.definition: A BPMNLabel is the DI element positioning the text label of a shape or edge, so names can be placed independently of the element they describe.
A waypoint is an (x, y) point on a BPMNEdge; the ordered list of waypoints defines the polyline the connection follows.
concepts.when_to_use: at least a start and end waypoint are needed for an edge to render.

concepts.definition: A Bounds gives the x, y position and width, height of a shape within a BPMNShape, defining where and how large the element is drawn.
isMarkerVisible on an exclusive gateway's BPMNShape controls whether the 'X' marker is drawn inside the diamond.
concepts.when_to_use: some tools hide the X on exclusive gateways; this attribute records that choice.

concepts.definition: isExpanded on a sub-process's BPMNShape indicates whether the sub-process is drawn expanded (internal flow visible) or collapsed (a '+' marker).

contrast.how: isExpanded=false corresponds to a collapsed sub-process shown with a plus marker; isExpanded=true shows the internal flow.

concepts.definition: isHorizontal on a pool's BPMNShape indicates whether the pool (and its lanes) is laid out horizontally or vertically.
potentialOwner is a resource role on a user task naming the set of people who are allowed to claim and complete the task.
concepts.when_to_use: to define the candidate group/role for a human task.

concepts.definition: humanPerformer is a resource role assigning responsibility for a task to a human resource, a specialisation of the generic performer.

contrast.how: a humanPerformer is generally responsible for the task, while a potentialOwner specifically may claim it from a work list.

concepts.definition: A resourceRole associates an activity with the resource (and optionally an assignment expression) responsible for performing it.
concepts.when_to_use: to bind a task to who performs it at runtime.

concepts.definition: participantMultiplicity indicates that a pool represents multiple instances of a participant (e.g. many customers), with minimum and maximum counts.
concepts.notation: a multi-instance (three-bar) marker on the participant pool.

concepts.definition: A subConversation groups a set of related conversations into a higher-level conversation node in a conversation diagram.
concepts.notation: a hexagon with a '+' marker.

concepts.definition: messageFlowRef links a conversation (or choreography element) to the specific message flows it summarises in a collaboration.
A categoryValue is the value a Group references to categorise the elements it visually encloses, enabling grouping by a shared category such as a cost centre.

contrast.how: a group is the visual boundary drawn on the diagram, while its categoryValue is the underlying category it represents.
